By STELLA HULT Star Correspondent Editor's Note: This is the third of a four part series on early days in Searchmont.
SEARCHMONT In August,1904, William O'Brien and Charles Keenan purchased the Searchmont Hotel from the Algoma Commercial Company. It exchanged ownership in March,1906 when Peter Sundstrum bought and operated the hotel until his demise in 1952.It was then managed by his daughter, Mrs. William Norman (Bertha) until 1956 when W.W.
Graham of Winnipeg. Man., became the new owner.
His is married to the former June Huckson, granddaughter of A.H. Huckson, who was a gov erm ment scaler anda popular figure in this area, in the early days of this century.
They have three children, Patrice, Andrea and Michael.
Previous to 1920, those wishing to cross the Goulais River, had to walk ecross the railroad bridge.A Mr. Brooks had a type of scow, and would

ferry one over the river for a nominal fee, but not too many took advantage of this type of transportation.A representative of the Algoma Central Railway was sent out once a year to top folk from using the bridge, thereby reminding them that they were trespassing on company property. Inthe winter of 1920 the department of highways constructed a bridge across the Goulais River.
The highway to Searchmont in 1924.Before this time, the was built during the term of office of he late James Lyons road from the Sault extended and the only access to Searchmont was by rail. Became By STELLA HULT Sault Star Correspondent SEARCHMONT-While attending the annual Christmas bazaar and tea held recently at the local hall, I was amaz- time.
ed at the great changes that A have been made this past summer. the Ihave teen absent from the community for the past few months and wasn't aware of the renovations and improve mev: being done. True enough minor changes have the been done from time to time, but they just didn't seem so noticeable as the alterations that took place this past summier.
Sipping my coffee and talking to Mildred Ulch, one of the original members, I remarked how much the club has grown aad prospered since its inception in 1954.
The Community Club, was born out of necessity. Although the school board in the year 1953-54 was aware that roof.
many improve meats and repairs were needed to the oneailed

room school, it wasn't in a position financially to do so.A new roof was sorely needed, the desks were in disrepair and the interior hadn't been redecorated for quite some wife of one of the trustees, in that year, with consent of the school board, decided to arrange for summer  dances to be held.
The community was also lacking social activity and it was thought that"two birds could be killed with one stone”.In village were amateur musicians who gave of their time and talents gratis. The late Walter Tessier, violin, his daughter Gloria(row Mrs.
"Skip"Thorp)of the Sault, piano and Larry Wagner, guitar provided the music, Dance floor wax, lighting (gas lamps) tickets and admissions were taken care of by Mrs. Lee Hult. The project proved quite successful, for enough funds were raised to buy the aluminum for a new But, it was quite a tiring job for so few because in order to have a dance the awkward desks had to be carried down to the basement and the next day the floor

dances, bingos, raffles, card parties, bazaars to name a few. The money was spent in various ways. When a resident of our area was in hospital a basket of fruit and other treats were sent, a new baby was welcomed to town with a gift of an eiderdown baby blanket. At the ena of the sc tool year awards were given a boy and girl of each grade with perfect attendance to try to discourage absenteeism. The few times when fire destroyed a home, a community shower was arranged.a dance neld with all proceeds given to the unfortunate ones.
Picnics were arra lig ed with races and games and refreshments given the children at the completion of a school year as well as skating and toboggan parties in the wintertime. Teen-age dances provided recreation for this particular age group. In 1956,35modern desks were installed in the school as well as a new desk and chair for the teacher. This equipment is now used in the new school. The interior of the school was painted by members of the club.
With the advent of Weldwood of Canada locating in Searchmont, and the influx of new residents, new four-

room school was built in 1960.
The one room school went up for bids, it was purchased by the club in 1961, and is now know ii as the Searchmont Community hall.
The school board by now needed no further assistance so the members concentrated their efforts to improve the interior of the newlv-acquired recreation centre. An addition was built to be used asa coffee bar and a frig and propane stove installed.
Yes, indeed the com mi unity club has done well but this summer has seen a coin ple te face-lifting at the local recreation certer. Through the generosity ofa Sault firm, enough paint was donated to redecorate the exterior. The club purchased aspenite for the ceilings of both the hall proper and the coffee bar as well as tangerine bamboo drapes for all windows.A new stage was constructed.
The club is indebted to Weldwood of Canada fora contribution of panelling for the walls. The carpenter work was done by several men of the area, especially John Scott who gave a great deal of his time to make the Searchmont Community hall an inviting looking place to relax, in during leisure hours.

media.text:
Searchmont Community Centre opens

A dream comes true Anewly-laid cornerstone of the Searchmont Community club is admired by vice-president, Elaine Lecuyer; president, Shirley Benedict; and secretary-treasurer, Millie Ulch. Directors are: Paul and Lois Burton, David Lecuyer, Verley Randell, Jacqueline Sisson, Melvin Sherlock, Glen Sundstrom, and Albert Tessier.

BY
JOHANNA
BISHOP ING
Special To The Star SEARCHMONTN- Nine months to a year ago, it did not seem possible, but they got it together, and hereitis, vyingfor attention with the Weldwood smoke stack: the bright, new Searchmont Community Centre, along held dream come true.
About 20 years ago, Marguerite Quinn, Betty Sundstrom, Alberta Tessier Mildred Ulch and Eila Sundstrom formed the Searchmont Community Club(SCC).
Mostofthe original executive members were present on Saturday to hear congratulatory messages and best wishes from Lance Bisch, representing the ministry of culture and recreation; Algoma MP Dr.
Maurice Foster; Bud Wildman, Algoma MPP; Wayne Pickard, school trustee; Juhani Pulkkinen, of Weldwood and recreation committee; Marsh Barsanti.representing Sault Mayor Nick Trbovich: Al Tessier.board oi directors

oftheSCC; and Rev. Father Rent, who is said to have some special connections.
From their messages it became apparent what difficulties theSCCfaced in getting the centre, from mountains of red tape to financing.
If there is one person in Searchmont who hasn ouse for red tape and who can wring money from a stone alias the board of education it appears to be Mildred Ul ch who was praised for her determination and perseverance by speaker after speaker. Both she and Little Al Tessier received a gift in recognition of their services. Both agreed, though, that without the massive backing of the whole community they could have accomplished little.
Highlight of the opening ceremonies was the laying of the cornerstone, containing a history of the events which led to the centre. Rev. Jerry Smith led those gathered outside in prayer.
The Finnish people of Sault Ste. Marie and the

Scottish Dancersof Bruce Mines added a splash of color to the opening festivities as they performed to the music of their native countries. Singer Pirjo Et ela niemi delighted the audience with solo performances. She presented a hand-woven wall hanging to the SCC.
Local talent added the distinctive touch  that reflected the diversity of this northern community.
Teacher Walter Sen ko was instrumental in getting some young artist son their way.
The new kitchen facilities were used for the first time, anda stream of irresistible dishes emerged from them for a delicious buffet supper.
During supper, stories were traded about the old community centre. Since 1924, it had served Searchmont, Wabos and Northland as school where Grades 1 to10were taught by a fondly remembered teacher who was not at all averse to using punishment to'enforce discipline. In the early60stheschoolbecame

the community hall which was expanded in1962to include a kitchen. The kitchen addition has found a new home: Amy Eatonhas adopted it.
Many people who donated their time and talent to raise money for the old and the new hall were present in Searchmont on Saturday. Among them were Larry Wagner and "Country Mama'and Dave Lezert. The old hall did have its charms, but its facilities were rather limited.
When Bud Graham's Hotel burned down, the need for asocial gathering place became acute. The new centre will fulfill many duties and will become the focal point of community activities, from physical education in conjunction with the school, to a home for the bustling New Horizon club. Many groups who were hampered in their growth by a lack of space will be able to expand now and, by helping to finish the newhall and using it, they will make truly their -and their community's-own.

media.text:
The Story of Searchmont begins with Francis Hector Clergue Clergue was born in Maine and later became a businessman and entrepreneur who arrived in Sault Ste, Mariein 1894.
Hecreated an industrial empire in Sault Ste. Marie and Algoma, that included a Steel Manufacturing Company, HydroElectric Power Company, Pulp and Paper Company, and Algoma Central&Hudson Bay Railway. The town of Goulais(later named Searchmont) was built asa model townsite complete with a park, which Clergue hoped would be usedto build other settlements along the railway right of way.
A sawmill was built on the banks of the Goulais River, and charcoal kilns were built near the base of the existing Ski Resort. The sawmill provided lumber to build the settlement, and the charcoal kilns provided charcoal which was used in the steelmaking process.

GOULAIS CHANGED
TO SEARCHMONT
One-hundred and Forty-five Families are now Settled in one township Nearby The name of Goulais Station on the ed to Searchmont, in honor of T.C. Algoma Central Railway has been chang Search, treasurer of the Lake Superior Consolidated, Great progres is being made this year ina quite way in the settlement of the Algoma Central's lands. Already the the whole of Gaudette township.near Searchmont Station, with the exception of a very small portion has been divided up and to-day 145 families are at work doing pioneer work there. All the settlers are delighted with their new properties, and good judges say the richness of the land is not excelled in Canada

Searchmont was named in honor of Theodore C. Search (1841-1920) Mr. Search served in various positions at the Consolidated Lake Superior Company(The parent company of the Lake Superior Pulp and Paper Company)which hada presence in Searchmont. Mr. Search served as Secretary Treasurer, VicePresident and Director. As the story goes, Francis H. Clergue who founded the Consolidated Lake Superior Company brought Search to the area on the railway and told Mr.Search that if he could secure money from investors for his Company the town would be named in his honor. This happened and the town became known as Searchmont. Mr. Search was aren owned American businessman who was the president of the National Association of Manufacturers, a founder of Philadelphia University and managing director of the Stetson Hat Company.

media.text:
New Building Is Booming SEARCHMONT-Construction valued at thousands of dollars is underway in a building boom which has reached this area lately.
The largest project is the new school on which work is progressing at a favorable rate.
The aluminium building has plenty of large windows which face Highway 556.
Don Gratton is just putting the finishing touches to a new two-storey chicken house in which he will house his large flock of birds.
Additions are being made to the Allan Roberts and Oscar Boyer homes and the materials for Larry Wagner's new home have been delivered to the site Construction is expected to get started soon.
The Searchmont Hotel has built an addition designated·for office space and Mr.and Mrs.
K. Leed and family have moved into their new home on the road behind the mill.
PERSONALS
Ernie Johnson is able to be out again after a severe case of hepatitis.
Mrs. Wagner was able to leave hospital and is convalescing at the home of her daughter in the Sault. Alex Olar is confined to bed with a back injury. Mr. Olar is much improved but the doctor has another week.

Sault Star Correspondent SEARCHMONT Alittle white schoolhouse trimmed in red? A red school house trimmed with spotless white? Or a little shack of withered logs backed by a clear blue sky? ranks.
The color scheme is not important-it was a stronghold of a civilization in a primitive land. Within its walls devoted men and women dispensed a heritage of learning. Under its roof, cherished traditions from scores of countries mingled and merged. It was the cradle of a nation growing up.

Schoolmates stand in for Grade 5-6 class as students ride tour train through S earchmont

Faithful class sees own sign from tour train

BY NILA TRUMBLE
Special To The Star SEARCHMONT-Itstill goesoneverymorningatg o'clock sharp in Searchmont. As the Agawa Canyon tour train rolls through the town, the passengers are greeted by Glen Atkinson's Grade 5-6 class from the Searchmont public school, toting signs and waving "Good Morning, drop us a

line. The ritual has been going on for four years. On Friday morning, Oct. 11, the5-6class was not there to wave. Instead, the entire school was emptied of students and teachers onto the highway in front of the school, along with parents and friends, as the tour train made its run through Searchmont. On this day, Mr. Atkin-

son and his class were passengers on the train, courtesy of the ACR and previous fans who had waved back from the train on their way to the canyon.
A'free breakfast and lunch were served to the students on the train and at 4:30 p.m.they were dropped off at Searchmont, a stop not usually on the train's tour schedule.

SEARCHMONT-Pierreand The Kids said thanks to Glenn Atkinson's Grades5and6class here Monday at Searchmont central public school.
Responding to hospitality given his family during an area visit Sept. 25, Prime Minister Trudeau wrote his appreciation ina letter to Searchmont-area students.
The letter, which arrived at the school Monday morning, thanked the students for their "warm and special' welcome while the the Trudeau family was passing through Searchmont during the visitors’Algo-

ma Central Railway(ACR)fall color tour trip to Agawa Canyon.
The Prime Minister also expressed his appreciation for the stories and smelly stickers the students gave to his sons.
"They (his sons) liked the pizza-flavored smelly stickers, plus the licorice and banana cream pie (stickers),'he wrote.“we also enjoyed the stories and paintings very much. You all deserve an A for effort."
Mr. Atkinson, whose students have received more than100 letters from ACR train riders

after being welcomed through Searchmont with a‘Good Morning' sign, said his class was site. wondering if they would receive a response from the Prime Minister.
"We're really excited the letter was personalized. It wasn't a form letter,"he said.“I told the class it'sreallysomething. Sept. 26.
Mr. Trudeau concluded his letter by telling the students he and his sons‘treasured your welcome and kind words.' The Prime Minister, along with his sons Justin, Sacha and Michel, spent the majority of their eight-hour stay in the their response.

Ernst Adolph Sjostedt, an eminent mining engineer and metallurgist, was aboard he RMS Titanic, the luxury passenger liner that sank after striking an Atlantic iceberg on its maiden voyage.
The 59-year-old, who was travelling second-class, boarded the White Star Line vessel in Southampton, England, on Wednesday, April 10, 1912.
He paid 13 pounds,10 shillings for his ticket to travel on what was then called the world's greatest ship, the "un sinkable”Titanic.
Thevessel, carrying2,209 passengers and crew, hit the iceberg at 11:40 p.m.on April 14.
At 2:20 a.m.on April 15, it sank in3,000metres of water, 350nautical miles southeast of Newfoundland.
On April 16, The Sault Daily Star, reported Sjostedt was believed to be among the passengers on the ship.

media.text:
The Story of Searchmont begins with Francis Hector Clergue Clergue was born in Maine and later became a businessman and entrepreneur who arrived in Sault Ste, Mariein 1894.
Hecreated an industrial empire in Sault Ste. Marie and Algoma, that included a Steel Manufacturing Company, HydroElectric Power Company, Pulp and Paper Company, and Algoma Central&Hudson Bay Railway. The town of Goulais(later named Searchmont) was built asa model townsite complete with a park, which Clergue hoped would be usedto build other settlements along the railway right of way.
A sawmill was built on the banks of the Goulais River, and charcoal kilns were built near the base of the existing Ski Resort. The sawmill provided lumber to build the settlement, and the charcoal kilns provided charcoal which was used in the steelmaking process.

Searchmont Personality

O. Boyer, Guide, Trapper Covers 6000mile Area

By DOROTHEA OLAR Sault Star Correspondent SEARCHMONT-Oscar Boyer, our personality this week is a well known figure in this area having spent a lifetime guiding and trapping from his camp at Pangis on the ACR.
Winters and holidays were spent in Sault Ste. Marie or Searchmont.
Mr. Boyer was born at Pangis, Oct.21,1901, where his father was in the lumbering business for Abitibi Pulp and Paper Co.
His father remained with the ACR.
Abi tibi Company until  1920.
He took ill while still at Pangis and was unable to walk out to the track. This necessitated a month-long wait for the ice

lake to board the train for the trip to the Sault. He died shortly after in hospital there. Mr. Boyer's mother, who is in her nineties, resides at a home for the aged in Toronto.
Oscar has one sister, the widow of Ben Nelson who was drowned at Batch awan a River in 1944.Mrs. Nelson lives in the Sault. Mr. Boyer is well known locally as well as by those who patronized his tourist resort which he owned and operated at Pangis, Mile 69, The area covered by Boyer's expeditions, comprises6,000 sguare miles of Algoma bush land, inaccessible by car or train. The area also boasts 85

speckled trout have been taken out of here that weigh seven and three-quarter pounds.
Conducted hunt in trips for moose, deer and bear in season were also offered by this famous Canadian guide and trapper.
He also trained the Indian and French Canadian guides he employed. They became experts in wood lore and catering to the needs of the outdoor sportsman. This 6,000 square miles of virgin territory in Algoma's "sportsman's wonderland"has been covered from end to end by Mr. Boyer personally by canoe and portage.
It is with regret that Oscar

was closed on ACR property He moved to Searchmont late in 1958 with his wife, the former Blanche La France, of Pembroke, their sons Oscar, Jr. aged18 8and eight-year-old Kenny, To Mr. Boyer it was like coming back home when he moved once again to Searchmont. When he was a youngster he spent winters here with his parents, and remembers some of the oldest buildings in our town being built.
He says the only church in our town the little white Roman Catholic Church on the hill, was built ir 1922 when he, along with several other fa mili ies, donated the money for the build-

THE HERMIT WHO LIVED IN RAGS THOUGH RICH
By: Lorna and Jamie Harris Illustration By: Bill McGrath of The London Free Press NEws ITEM: A recluse, who hunted wolves in the bush north o6 Sauet Ste. Marie until he was 81, has left the interest from a $180,000 trwst fund to East Elgin District High School in Ayemer.
Richmond "Bob" Beck, 90, who died last January in a Sauet Ste.
Marie retirement home, spent his youth in Springfield, near Aylmer. when he died, Mr. Beck had no relatives except distant cousins.
Searchmont, Bob Beck's home for more than seven decades...settled in the broad valley of the Goulais River north of the Sault...its industrial focal point, the Weldwood Mill whose water-tower is dwarfed by the surrounding tree covered mountains...the slopes and chalets on its southern outskirts, well known to ski enthusiasts...
On a sultry summer night, in the wilderness of the Algoma district, most of the resident activity is centred on the laundromat or the hotel. The main diversion for an out-of-towner would be to go down to the Algoma Central Railway tracks and listen to the rails as they groan and bang while cooling off from a day in the sun.
Known as "the hermit", Bob Beck could be seen on such a night, alone with his thoughts, as he made his way through the twilight.
He used to shuffle along the gravel shoulier of the Searchmont highway From the railroad track, he followed the curve in the road past the general store and off toward the river. His face, at least as much as was visible from under the battered old hat, was black with filth. His patched and re patched clothes had lost their original color under a uniform layer of gray dirt.
He turned up the river road, bent slightly under the heavy sack strung over his shoulder.A dusty half-mile later, he arrived at a shack set back slightly in the woods. The hillsides were gold and green and silent with the evening, as Bob Beck opened the door and was swallowed up by the dark interior of his home.
of his bequest, it would have been no surprise to the hermit's former neighHis shack, however, gave no hint of its owner's affluence. It was half hidden behind piles of wood and a huge heap of old tires. The shack was erected on the property of a school teacher who had left the area but continued to pay the taxes.
Bob made most of the contents. The stove was a series of tin cans and drums he had assembled. All of his utensils were fashioned out of scraps of wood and metal..He could be seen, almost daily, visiting the local junk piles; he found uses for things anybody else would discard.
Bob's personal appearance wasa product of his frugal lifestyle. The pile of tires outside his shack accounted for the colour of his skin--he burnt them in his stove. This kept him black especially in the winter when the temperatures would drop to 50-below zero, preventing proper yen til ation and rendering bathing impossible.

media.alt: Bob Beck doc page 2 of 3_edited_edited.p
media.text:
Bob Beck first came to the Searchmont area in 1906 when he secured a job as a surface worker for Superior Mines. The mines, now known as Copper Crest, are situated near Wabos, another Algoma village about l0 miles from Searchmont.
At that time, there were 50 men employed at the site. The highest wages were 25 cents an hour. Bob, however, as a surface worker, would have received only $1.75fora10-hour day.
During the First World War, Bob spent three years in the army. He joined the ll9th Battalion of the Sault Ste. Marie Regiment. Drafted into the 42nd Battalion in France, he served as a sniper as well as an operator of a Lewis gun.
a lot of close shaves." His battle experience, however, left him without his sense of taste, the fact which explains his ability to consume the awful conglomerations which he used to cook on his home-made stove. In 1916, while at training camp in England, Mr. Beck placed first in a target-shooting match. Princess Louise, sister of King George V, presented him with a silver-tipped cane. Through the years this cane passed from hand to hand among various residents of the Searchmont area.
When the war was over, Bob returned to Searchmont in order to maintain a postoffice address. (The Searchmont Post Office is the only one within 30 miles to the south and 100 miles in any other direction.) But, not all of his business could be conducted through the mails. For many years it was his custom to make a monthly trip into the Sault in order to do his banking and other business. Onefall day while he was waiting for the bus, he was clipped by a hit-and-run driver. .
He maintained his silence and got onto the bus but, by the time he arrived in the Sault, he could hardly walk because of a hip injury. A policeman, taking him for a drunk, picked him up as he staggered along Queen Street.
by the police. Even though he used to take off one layer of grime before visiting the Sault, he still looked like a tramp.
The police, threatening him with vagrancy charges, thought that he was fooling when he demanded that they contact his banker. Finally they relented.
The banker rushed over and secured the release of his friend and client. After ahasty explanation of the elderly man's financial status and physical condition, the threats were withdrawn and Bob was rushed off to hospital for treatment.
Although no bones were broken, he was kept in hospital for two weeks and· spent the balance of the winter with friends in the Sault.A much cleaner hermit returned to his shack the following spring only to find that vandals had ransacked his belongings and his rifles had been stolen. Through all his years in Searchmont, Bob had various types of employment.
He worked at bush camps and lumber mills besides doing a great deal of trapping and gardening.
By the time he had left Searchmont to enter a retirement home in the Sault, he was over 80 years old and estimated that he had trapped scores of wolves..In fact, his pride and joy, a five-string home-made banjo, was faced with wolf skin.
o he inherited his money from a sister, Mrs. Olive May Van Schoonhoer, who lived in Detroit up until her death in l965.Others maintain that his fortune was based on the sale of the original family homestead in Southern Ontario, augmented through the years by profits from real estate holdings in and around Sault Ste. Marie.
Although secretive in his habits, Bob was moved by the suffering of other people. One time he joined a search party north of Searchmont after a young lad had been reported missing from the lumber camp. Five hundred men combed

media.text:
o s bear had attacked and killed the lad. From that time until bears were protected by law, Bob trapped them with a vengeance.
Up until the last few years of his life, Bob used to go to the Algoma Central Railway station with an old bear skin. Whenever a tourist-filled train would pull in, he would drape the skin over himself and parade around the platform to advertise the fact that this was the big bear district of Algoma.
He e used to have shacks scattered throughout the surrounding mountains. He also planted a good number of apple trees off in the woods. Every fall he would carry the harvest out on his back. He would peddle some of the apples to his neighbors.
About once a year, the old hermit would drop in on each of his friends to reminisce, play his banjo and sing a few songs.
In return, his neighbors provided him with refreshment and second-hand newspapers to read to keep up with the times.
On Sunday, July 25,1965, to celebrate his 80th birthday, Bob's close friends gave him a party at the home of Lee Hult in Searchmont. It was his first birthday party in 65 years. The Sault Star reported that Bob took the opportunity to play several selections on his banjo including The March of the 42nd Battalion, one of his owm compositions.
Sir Adam Beck, the great uncle of the Searchmont hermit should be well known to Londoners. He was a mayor of London from 1902 to 1904and an MLA from 1905 until 1919.He also established the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario of which he was the chairman until his death in 1925.The innate Beck spirit for pioneering ran strong whether in the relatively civilized surroundings of Southwestern Ontario or in the wilderness of the Algoma district of northern Ontario.

EAR-SCRATCHING A HOBBY
Here isa photograph of a one-antlered moose that suffers considerably with flies about the head, according to statement of Bob Beck, Searchmont trapper, who took the picture. The animal, so he says, is crazy to have his head scratched and will dispute the roadway with bushman in pursuit of some obliging individual. It i felt that his hobby may lead to a violent end at the hands of some hunter this fall.

Bob reminded  us that in those days there was “no such thing as unemployment insurance so a guy had to dig." Eventually big boilers were moved into the mine and men were hired to cut cord wood to run the new steam-operated machines. Arailroad ands was also built intn the mine but the price of copper dropped so drastically that soon all operations were halted.
Bob Beck spent three years in the Army during the First World  War. He joined the 119th Battalion of the Sault Ste. Marie Regiment but was drafted to the 42nd in France.
Some of his duty in France was as a sniper but mostly he was on Louis guns, a type of machine gun.
He said "Iwasnever wounded but sure had lots of close shaves.' In 1916, while still in England at a training camp with his original battalion, he entered a target shooting competition and won the shoot off. He was presented with a silver-tipped cane by Princess Louise, a sister of King George V.
The cane is still in a home at Searchmont.
Quite a few years ago, Bob recalls that he gave the cane to Dave Jones who at that time lived at the Charlie Thorp home. Upon his death the cane passed to C. Wilson.
When Mr. Wilson died a few years ago  the cane again passed into new hands.
In the years since the end of the First World War, Mr.
Beck has maintained a home at Searchmont so as to have a Post Office address. He says it's the only Post Office within 30 miles up one direction and a hundred in the other.

The hotel was already flourishing here and a Mr. Naylor was operating a general store on the adjacent lot.
The Algoma Commercial Company had a mill at Searchmont but found the 12mile-per-hour current too swift for their type of operation so the mill was eventually moved to the Sault. Mr. Becktold us ofa cousin who was knighted by Queen Victoria. He couldn't tell us just why this honor was bestowed but Sir Adam Beck was born at Baden, Ontario and educated at Galt Grammar School. He Mayor of London Ontario 1902- was 04 and a member of the Provincial Legislature,1905-19.
Our encyclopedia says Sir Adam Beck was a “Canadian financier and statesman. He sponsored the establishment of the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario and was its  chairman  until his death'.(He died in 1925).
The encyclopedia also says "Knighted in 1914."
Sunday, July 25was Bob Beck's 80th birthday and he was honored  at a birthday party at the Lee Hult home at Searchmont.
Mrs. Hult baked and dec orated a large birthday cake Mr. Beck told us this was his complete with candles and first birthday party in65 years.
He played several selections on his banjo -oneofhis favorites 1 played several times “Marchof the42nd Battalion' seemed to bring back many memories of war days.
Leisure hours are  spent playing the banjo and enjoying the antics of a pet squirrel.

Ialso knew the Stover spoken of when I was a kid of thirteen it was at this age I started to camp John R.(as Stover was known was then) superintendent for the E.F. Loud company who owned and operated a narrow gauge railway Cown as the Au Sable and Northwestern about sixty miles north of Bay City.
Imet him again in the camps back of Blind River, his son, whom we all know as Stub was elected after the previous world war as M.P.P.from Blind River.
The James Cosgrove mentioned was at Wild which I think is now Northland in the year of 1904 as foreman in the bush. Mike a brother of Jimwasone of our old fighting shanty men. Charlie Keenan who until his death managed the Royal Hotel at the corner of Gore and Queen was at this time proprietor of the Searchmont hotel.
-一 This I think was the year after the Steel Plant strike and we all received our checks monthly from the Algoma Commercial company, at least I think this was the name they operated under.
In order to get our checks cashed we must purchase something and what more could we purchase at an hotel than liquor.I was a cookee at this time and our cook was a real booze artist. When pay day arrived we gave the tote teamster our checks, that is the cook, myself and another cookee. Also a gallon container which was filled for $3.When that arrived it meant, we the cooke es would get breakfast and dinner the following day and as most of the gang sent checks out and also received liquid refreshments abig celebration was the result. As often happened a big fight was in progress, and possibly a portion of the crew wound up in Searchmont to stay until the month's wages were gone.
IfI remember right the camps in this vicinity that winter numbered four under the foreman sip of Cameron Beck for whom Iworked, George Pyette, Charlie Gaudette and Tom Scott. The first two mentioned have since passed away.
Billy Parks who died a year ago

Sault Daily Star Feb 25 and who acted as foreman employed by the Lake Superior Paper Company and in later years by the Abitibi was at this time a teamster and top-notch hook man.
- Searchmont though only bcasting one hotel was a stop over place for this Jack going in and coming out.
Bright-eyed men, tall and straight slike the trees with which they labored coming in from the camps by the old tote road shouldered their way 1through the milling crowd up to the one bar the town boasted to geta glow on while waiting for the train twhich would carry them to the Soo.
-O
I don't think there was any vocation in life unless it be the builders of railroads that allows one to view more beautiful scenery than that of the camp life, yet it was all unobserved by them. It was their natural environment and Nature's canvas depicting beautiful sunrises or sunsets meant nothing to them.
Yet they had little or no opportunity to view any of Nature's expositions as the rise and setting of the sun found them busy, heads bowed to their tasks.
The beauty spots on the river were the most dangerous. We might take for instance the Serpent back of Blind River and pick out what was known as the Improvements. First there was the Chute from the upper dam that emptied its waters into the pond just above what was known as the Blind Dam, here there was an eddy on each side of the stream, the larger one on the right hand side facing up stream. The Chute of possibly a hundred feet or more at an incline of 35 or more degrees, shot logs down at express train speed and dove down endwise out of sight; and up again with such force they nearly left the water. From here they were carried to another chute a short distance below where they were again hurled through a churning cauldron toat last float into the quiet waters below.
This place where waters leaped into the air for many feet and broke to fall back in a shimmering spray, rainbow hued in the rising sun which lanced through the pearly swirlsof mist resembling silken bridal robes on the spreading out of a vast opalescent curtain.
Now the river that at one time overflowed its banks at flood time has deteriorated as have the pine tree forests. The hills are nude, their gaunt heads covered only by driet up moss as lifeless as a dead man's beard.

River Drivers -- Hot- Rods on Logs

Algoma's Hungry Sawmills Auait

The Big Push Spring Log Drive

Special to the Star TORONTO-There's a sense of urge ney, an atmosphere of expectancy along the ice-filled rivers of Northern Ontario as the fabulous river-drivers await the moment the logs begin to move. Spring drives are ai most ready to start and one Canada's most spectacular jobs about to begin.
True it is that trucks, tractors, railways have been carrying logs

from the pulpwood and lumber camps throughout the winter. But millions of board feet of logs have been pile on the ice of lakes or or the river banks ready for the roaring waters to move them toward the mill-ponds. To keep them moving are the drivers, some of them youngsters barely out of their teens, others veterans of a score of drives, many still celebrated in song and fireside legend th rc ugh out North-

ern Ontario.
There's hardly a major river in the north which doesn't have a log drive. The Upper Ottawa, the Mississauga, the Marten, the Pic, Nipigon, the Aguasabon, all float their valuable cargoes lakes on which mills are situated. 10 Here the logs are boomed, held for storage, pulled up the jack ladders into the mills to be sawn into lumber or crushed, beaten dissolved’for manufacture of a

thousand varieties of paper.
The rush to meet a newspaper deadline isn't any greater than is the hurry to move a log cut.
perfect; the moment the ice melts or goes out of lake or river, logs which have been either piled on the lake ice or along the banks of the river begin to move. Tliey must be kept moving, for only during the spring run-off, the high water,

can they be kept afloat.
Hang-ups-in which logs are stranded on shoals, are not only uneconomical but also call for tremendously heavy work. Log jams can be averted-sometimes by careful “feeding'’of the river. But despite man-made plans, they still happen and, in cases, they can hold up an entire drive. Hence the immediate call for skilled jam-breakers, men who can walk a rolling log as delicately and quickly as a cat, who can throw a cable loop around a key log with utmost skill or place a bundle of dynamite sticks in a strategic spot without turning a hair.
Despite advances in equip ment and technique, there still hasn't been much change in the equipment used on the log drive.
The load has been lessened to some extent by the use of aluminum for pike poles, the use of tractors instead of horses. But the drive still needs strong, skilled men who can wade in icy clothes from morning till night and can tell at a glance which logs are hoiding up the drive.
Top river drivers can glance at a river-even a strange river -and detect unfailingly just how booms should be placed to di favourable eddy or backwater; vert logs around obstacles, into how long a drive should take, almost to the minute, including the cleaning up process which sees the drivers with their stranded logs into faster and peavies andpikes moving deeper waters.

Some of them have never worked on any other river: some have worked every one from the Ottawato Lake of the Woods.
They work hard and they play hard-although there have been many changes since the old davs ofs30-a-month-and-found-for the skilled river driver of today is one of the highest paid men in the bush.
There are few tougher grinds than a major log drive. Food is served, in many cases.from a floating kitchen which accompanies the drives. In times of emergency the men may not even take time to eat for it is essential the logs be kept moving before the water subsides which may be overnight on some rivers.
Soon the northern rivers will be full of logs.the drives will be over and tho drivers again, as they have done for many years will celebrate the completion of the winter harvest of timber from Ontario's forest.

SEARCHMONT
SEARCHMONT LUMBER
DRIVE COMING DOWN
GOULAIS RIVER FAST
Searchmont, June 26.-The drive of the Searchmont Lumber Co. which was almost tied up for want of water is moving down the Goulais River at a fast rate, as the water is very high nOw.
The sawmill is again running, har ing started the summers cut last Saturday. Frair Rath, Lumber Co.of Glendale are hauling logs by tractor from Proulx's.camp.

Roberts, A Lacombe, E. Leclair, M. Nault, J.Mc Gregor, J. Seer, A.LaChapelle.
Mrs. A. Matthews made two trips to the Whitman Dam on Friday.

NUMBER OF JOBLESS
DECREASES: RIVER
DRIVERS WANTED
Sault Star Jun 6 1930 Seven Housemaids Needed But Cannot Be Obtained "The employment situation still re mains dull, but the number of app li cations for work.have decreased somewhat." Superintendent W. Hunt, of the Government Employment Bureau, told the Star this morning. Fourteen men were sent to Glendale to fight the bush fire there yesterday but as this fire is now out the men are back in town again looking for employment.
The river drives are demanding men for that work but they must be experienced. Fourteen were  sent to Mile 60, A.C.R.to work on the drive there, and there is still a vacancy for five more good drivers. Seven river drivers were sent to Searchmont also.

Sault Star May 15 1934 100,000 Logs to Come Down Garden River; Water High With a crew of15men leaving the Sault for Ranger Lake yesterday,75 river drivers are engaged in the Eastern Lumber Co.'s annuai irive down the Garden River.
In all there are100.000logstobe driven down the Garden River thig year fnomthe Ranger Lake area. That is half the cut last year when there were200.000logs.and much less than half of the largest cut in the area some years ago when 250, 000 logs were taken out.
Logs are now appearing at the mouth of the Garden. The drive is proceeding rapidly since there i6 plenty of water. Water in Ranger Lake is extremely high.

media.text:
RECALLS SOME OF ALGOMA'S

FAMOUS RIVER DRIVERS

Sault Star July 15 1938 Suggests PIO Games As Well As Log Rolling Contest By S.B.DICKINSON MONTREAL RIVER, July 9. (Received July 15.)-Iread an article in "The Star'a short time ago about Joe Casca net te and his ability on the river. Joe was as god a river man as ever donned a caulked shoe, but never has Joe accomplished this feat or any one else that I ever drove with. And this includes the old river drivers of both Michigan and Ontario who were second to none.
I never was any front page artist on a log but I have tried this stunt and have watched many other unsuccessful attempts. When the log upend ed we did also. If The Star wishes to get the low down on Casca net te just goup to Baldwin's Mill and ask for Murdock McDonald who worked with Joe in his palmy days.
The Soo district had many famous characters who followed this vocation. Here are a few: Dry Foot Sam, George McNee, whose son Jack lives on Bay Street, was one of the best white water men in the district, not so much on logs but as a forman, he understood water; Slippery Dan, a brother of Murdock; Bunk-bound Ryan

Walking Daly: Seven Day Whalen. My own nickname was acquired on the Au Sable River back of Massey.I was riding a homestead, so called on account of its unusual size, and when you fall off a log bearing this cognomen you aren't much ofa driver. But I did and when I came to the surface the boss asked where I'd been.“Looking for fish tracks I replied. So the name "Fish Track Dick" stuck to me for the remainder of the season.
The Star also suggested putting on a log rolling contest, why not add all of the old games played in the camps including shanty songs, poetry, step dancing, and so on.I think some of the old timers could give good entertainment.
Ihave two letters which I have kept since the Great War, written from somewhere in France which I will submit later or a copy as I would not part with the originals. One is from one of the boys in the vernacular of the camps and another from our camp missionary's son who served with the boys."over there."

Vihtori Kallio, who came to Canada in 1909 at the age of 19, was presented with a Pioneer Medal of Honor on behalf of the Finnish Historical Soci ely of Sudbury. This organization which includes Finnish people of Sault Ste.
Marie, currently is compiling a history of Finnish people in Canada.lt is expected to be completed next year.
Presentation of the medal was made to Mr. Kallio Wednesday night in a program at St. Mary's Finnish Lutheran Church. Mr. Kallio did bush work out of Searchmont. He haswo.children, Mrs.
William Knuuttila(Aune)with home he lives here and a son, Walter of Searchmont.
The program, in Finnish, included selections by St.
Mary's church choir directed by Oliver Turpela and a group from the Finnish Pentecostal Betania church choir. Maria Hill gave a reading from the Kalevala.the Finnish national epos. Erkki Jokinen and Vilho Hyykylainen sang solos and Mr. Turpela performed on the organ.

media.text:
HOPE LUMBER CO.
TOOK 15,00,0 FT.
OUT THIS WINTER
About800 Men Employed In Their Camips In District Between 10,000,000 and 15,000,000 feet of pine and spruce logs have been taken out of the bush during the past Beason by the Hope Lumber Co.at their respective camps at Glendale, A.C.R.and Dean Lake$678,000re presenting the value of the logs and the cost of operations.
About 8o0 men altogether were employed by the company, about 350 taking care of the operations at Glendale, where between 7,000.000and 8,000.000 feet of logs were taken out, and 450 wen at Dean Lake where be tween10,000,000 and 12,000,000 feet of logs were taken out.
The value of logs and cost of op erations at Glendale amounted to approximately $290.000, and at Dean Lake, about $388.000.From Glendale the logs are driven down the Garden river'and transferred to the com pany's mill at Thessalon where they are made into lumber and sold com mercially. The logs from Dean Lake are driven down by way of the Mis sissauga river and transferred to the same mill.

With good luck the Hope Lumber Company off icl als believe they should have all their logs at the mill in Thessalon by July 1.About 15 per cent of the logs taken out by the Hope Lumber Company this season were spruce logs. It is understood that the cut this year is about the same as in other years.
It is expected that the camps will break up about the fifteenth of this month when practically all the men will go home for the balance of the winter. When the drive starts May, or as soon as the ice goes out and conditions are favorable, about 60men will be re employed at Glendale to conduct the drive, and about 125 will be employed at Dean Lake.
At the present time the men are confining their work to hauling the logs to the river and preparing them for the drive. At Glendale the company has a Phoenix hauler, with ca ter pillar wheel attachment whiehis operated by steam, and which hauls twenty sleighs of logs atone time.
This device takes care of the log haul at camp 5 and camp 7.Horses are used to haul logs from the other camps,

Searchmont Resort Is Success Story Searchmont Valley Ski Club is beginning to look more like the beau tif ui dream Ian McDonald and Herb Lederer have hung on to ever since they took an option on the Algoma mountain five or six years ago.
The pace quickened when the project became a company two years back and really picked up speed over the past summer.
With its altogether new look, the place begins to resemble the ski resorts you see in Ski magazine, It's still util it aran. The emphasis remains on family fun, promotion of young skiers and healthful winter exercise.
While the latest in ski togs and equipment is becoming common, it still is no status symbol at Searchmont. You rate if you enjoy yourself, are thoughtful of others on the hill, and are a genial companion for after-ski snacks in the new lodge (with inside plumbing, yet!) Therows of cars lining up behind the lodge and the steady stream of traffic over the 35 mile road from the Sault bringing spectators are proof that Searchmont is beginning to rate. Searchmont has had backing from a number of influential Sooites since the company was formed and most of them are using the resort as a form of family activity.
The first of many family chalets has been erected as a joint project by the Dr. Elgies and the Bill Adamses for a weekend residence.
Special fares for bus and train passengers have been arranged by ACR and Steel City Coaches. And best of all from the skiers' standpoint is tr.e new poma lift which whisks them nearly to the top of the mountain. The most enterprising then have more than a mile of splendid downhill runs.

Ski Trails

Searchmont Slopes

Attract All Ages

By DOROTHY OLAR Sault Star Correspondent SEARCHMONT-Fresh packed snow has improved condition on the slopes of Searchmont Valley Ski Resort. Condi tions were ideal Wednesday and the fresh snow and beautiful weather brought skiing fans out in car loads.
Mr. and Mrs. Henry Bullock, a husband and wife team from the Sault, make a very handsome pair- Henry in a dark outfit and Mary in avery smart Scandinavian pattern sweater and black slacks, The Herb Lederer's were out in force. Daughter Jackie, aged five, and Herbie Jr., three years-old, are doing very well on skis.
Wee Robert aged two says "Daddy, I want skis too," SO probably before long he'll be joining the rest of the family on the slopes.
Echo Bay Mrs. Wilfred Everett of Little Current spent the weekend with her parents, Mr.and Mrs. Sam Graham.

Beginners hill is a real hive ofaetivity -beginner doesn't mean juniors only -we have them here from six to 60or more accurately-from three to65-with one thing in common, the first pair of skis. Herb Lederer is the capable instructor and is kept quite busy weekends and Wednesdays but as Herb says There is always room for one more. So let me issue an open invitation to anyone with a hankering to ski-don't put it off any longer, come out and join the fun. As the slogan says-don't wait till spring -do it now.
So nice to see familiar faces in the crowd. Last Sunday we noticed Lloyd Sundstrom among the spectators.
Lloyd is a former home towner having spent many years here when his family owned the Searchmont Hotel. Two sisters, Gertie, Ewan and Mabel Montgomery,(hope I'm right there) Mabel's husband Bob and Johnny Johnston made up the party. Fresh fallen snow assures a good weekend for skiing so folks "let's rally round the Pama-lift."

media.text:
Ski Club Opens

At Searchmont

The Searchmont Valley Ski Club opens its new hill to the public Sunday.
Ian MacDonald and Herb Led erer, who developed the location over the past summer, announced that the road to the lodge has been plowed clear of snow, and that a snack bar will be operated in the heated lodge. The hill can be seen on the right hand side of the road, just before entering Searchmont.
Thr road into the hill begins just after the Searchmont General store.
People that have seen the hill so far have been very pleased with its size and adaptability to all classes of skiers.
Snow conditions on the two developed runs couldn't be better. There are steep slopes and gentle slopes, and a slalom run that stands strictly for the expert.
The hill was previously packed well, only partway. But yesterday the boys worked hard packing the top part of the slope to comfortable wi td th, to suit the intermediate skier.
Groups of skiers have been out to the hill on the past few weekends, and an excellent crowd is expected to attend the opening of the location Sunday.
The lodge is heated now, after Herb and Ian brought two stoves into the log cabin lodge, Friday.

BY ALEX MITCHEL I
Of The Star Bill Autio hopes to begin a new victory streak Saturday when defending champion Diodati'sPowerliftingClubof Sault Ste. Marie hosts the Central Canadian Powerlifting championships.
The 32-year-old Autio, who has a string of six consecutive victories in the 242-pound class from meets dating back to November.1974, will enter the 220-pound category for Saturday's competitions.
Normally, the steel worker would have been considered a favorite in the 242-pound category, but when he contacted a severe stomach flu infection in April, Autio lost 25 pounds, During the sum mer he was only able to gain seven pounds leaving him around 220.
"I feel strong, but I have lost a little,"he admitted Tuesday.
But by dropping down a category, Autio is well within reach of establishing a total lift record in the 220-pound category.
Only one lifter has passed 1400-pounds in Canada. Autio did 1440-pounds at the Eastern Canadian championships Jan.12 in Quebec City. including 625 in the dead-lift.

Sault Star Correspondent SEARCHMONT-Forty three years of service with the Algoma Central Railway came to an end this fall when Eric Gratton retired.
Mr. Gratton spent 23 years with an ACR telephone line gang and 10 years with the mechanical department operating water tanks at Searchmont and Ogidaki. Another ten years were spent as a section hand at Searchmont after the railway installed diesel engines and water tanks were abandoned.
Hewas born in Birming-

to Canada in 1900with his parents and seven brothers and sisters.
In 1902 the family moved to Searchmont where John Bruce Gratton, Eric's dad, bought 190 acres from the railway and settled his family at an old set of logging camps about a mile up the track from the homestead.
The family remained there while Eric, his father and brothers cut the great cedar logs and built a large farm house now occupied by Don Gratton, an older brother.

in1923and in 1927 moved in with his bride, the former Normanda McIntyre of MacLennan. The Grattons have three three sons, Morris of the Sault, Wayne of Cornwall and Donald, deceased.
Mr. Gratton has not yet decided how to spend his time in retirement, but he and Mrs.
Gratton intend to spend some time with their son Wayne at Cornwall.
They have always enjoyed farming and plan to carry on,

P.T. Taylor Bailey an ACR employee retires.

media.text:
P. T. Taylor-Bailey New By DOROTHY OLAR Sault Sfar Correspondent SEARCHMONT -With the coming of the dial phone, many changes are evident in this community. One of the changes and possibly the greatest one is that the old switchboardisnowpasse.
With the passing of the switchboard your friend and mine.W.P. Taylor-Bailey, will go into semi- retirement.
After many years of faithful service Mr. Taylor-Bailey. or"P.T” as.he is fondly called by friends and acquaintances near and far, hopes to have time to relax and enjoy some fishing.
It might, he aid, that “P.
T"grew up in a railroading world. His father was in the railway supply business. His job was to upholster sleep cars and supply blinds for the coaches."P.T"entered the same career in 1905 when he

Telephones Force was employed by the Canadian Pacific in Montreal.
In 1916 he moved to Steelton in the employ of the Algoma Central Railway. In the many years of service he has worked in the Stores Department, as a switcher, on baggage and as station agent.
As station agent he worked at Hawk Junction to return to Searchmont then back to remained here since.
In1953the switchboard was moved from the station to a small house nearby and here“P.T"was on call:24 hours a day He recalls the days when Searchmont station was a very busy place. Tourist and fishermen would travel by car this far to catch ihe train and journey on up the line to their favorite camps and lakes. Now these places are easily accessible by car and so an era has passed.

Sault Star may 6 1963 Retirement Mrs. Taylor-Bailey is in charge of the postoffice in the the same building and carried out these duties intermittently since 1930.'She is very active in the Community Club and being a registered nurse is called on quite frequently to administer to young and old alike all times of the day or night."
The Taylor-Baileys have two daughters, Enid,(Mrs.
Tessier), who lives in the Sault and Marlene Mrs.
Johnston) at present in Tokyo, Japan, where her husband is stationed with the Air Force, S.A.C, division. His three years service there will be over in July and the Baileys anxiously await their homecoming.
There are four grandchildren and“p, T"looks forward, to spending many leisurely hours with them in the future.

media.text:
COMPLETE PHONE
LINE THIS WEEK
Sault Star Apr 23 1934 Provides Complete Forestry Branch Hookup in This Area Construe tion of the new forestry branch telephone line from Island Lake to Glendale will be completed by the end of this week, Chief Forest er Nigel Kensit told the Star in an interview today.
Necessary poles, brackets and insulatore are all up and the stringing of the line isabout half completed.
Work is being done by members of the forestry branch staff.
The new telephone line will complete the forestry branch circuit. Present lines extend from the Sault to Batch awan a, from Blind River-to Glendale via camp 18 and Ranger Lake. The Ieland-Lake Glendale stretch completes the hookup which takes in all headquarters and all towers.
